opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that I thought Google was a bad place. It's a great company with brilliant people. But when I imagined myself there, I could already see the whole path laid out: join a big team, own some small piece of a huge system, get promoted step by step, and in five or ten years I'd be doing more or less a bigger version of the same thing. It felt too predictable.

What excites me is being close to the frontier, where things are still messy and nobody really knows the answer yet. At a company that size, much of the infrastructure is already mature, and your impact is often incremental: optimizing something by a few percent, or maintaining something that already works. That's valuable, but it's not what makes me want to wake up in the morning.

I'd also spent a lot of time on open-source work and research. I liked building something from scratch, seeing people actually use it, and getting that direct feedback loop. I wanted a place where one person, or a small group, could move the needle, where what you build in a few months might actually change how the whole field does things. A smaller, more ambitious environment felt much more aligned with that.

So it was less "Google is boring" and more "I don't want to optimize for safety and stability at this stage of my life." When you're young, I think the best bet is to go where the most interesting problems are, even if it's riskier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he expected to own a small piece of a huge system on a predictable path, conveying the sense of being a cog in a large company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that Google itself was uninteresting as a company. It was more about what the role would have looked like for me at that stage. When I interviewed, the kind of work on the table felt very incremental, like you'd be owning one small piece of a huge, mature system, and the feedback loop between what you build and what actually ships could be months or years.

I'd just spent a lot of time building Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, mostly on my own, and that experience spoiled me a bit. I was used to having an idea in the morning, implementing it in the afternoon, and seeing people use it that week. So the thought of trading that for a lot of process and a narrow scope just didn't excite me.

The other thing was that I wanted to be somewhere RL and large-scale training were the main event, not one project among hundreds. At a big company you can absolutely find great teams doing that, but you're often competing internally for compute and attention. I wanted a place where the entire organization was pointed in the same direction I cared about, where being a strong systems and infrastructure person directly moved the research forward. That's why a smaller, more focused lab like OpenAI was a much better fit for me at the time.

r001.rationale: The response says the role would mean owning one small piece of a huge, mature system, which conveys feeling like a cog in a large company.

astra-6.text: It wasn’t really about Google specifically. I was more excited by the idea of building something from scratch, where I could help decide what to work on and see the impact of my decisions. Google might have been a great opportunity, but it wasn’t the kind of experience I was looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says Jiayi wanted to build from scratch and shape the work, but it does not identify feeling like a cog in a large company as a reason Google seemed uninteresting.

sol-6.1.text: I think it was less about Google itself and more about what I wanted from my work. It’s an impressive company, but the prospect of joining a big organization didn’t excite me as much as building something where I could help decide what to do and why. I was more interested in that uncertainty and ownership than in having a recognizable name on my résumé.

r001.rationale: The response says joining a big organization felt unexciting because she wanted ownership and a say in what to do, conveying the concern about being a cog in a large company.
